paragraphs: Friend, here's what David's prayer teaches me: God wants your whole life, not just your emergency requests. David opens with "I call upon You, O LORD; come quickly to me" (Psalm 141:1), and then he asks for his prayer to be "like incense" (Psalm 141:2). I think he wants his prayer to rise up as something sweet, and not only a loud alarm. And then he gets personal, asking the LORD to "Set a guard" over his mouth and to keep his heart from being drawn to any evil thing (Psalm 141:3-4).

Now here's the part that gets me. David asks to be corrected, and he calls a righteous man's rebuke "an act of loving devotion" and "oil for my head," then adds, "let me not refuse it" (Psalm 141:5). That's a prayer for a soft heart before the correction even shows up! I'd like to say I'm that humble, but my own hands are still waving a little "I KNEW that" when somebody tells me my oven's running hot. So the lesson is simple: a person who really wants to stay close to God makes room for loving correction.

Then the psalm gets dark, with traps, snares and "our bones have been scattered at the mouth of Sheol" (Psalm 141:7). But one little word turns it around: "But my eyes are fixed on You, O GOD the Lord. In You I seek refuge" (Psalm 141:8). David doesn't pretend the danger isn't real. He just keeps his eyes on the LORD and asks Him to keep him from the traps, and that's where the baker's safety is too.
